name: PaaS platform
title:
Services in
one interface
summary: A platform interface, automated cloud operations and repeatable delivery of changes.

chapters.label: PROBLEM
chapters.title:
Code needs
an operating environment
chapters.text: Launching a service takes more than code: it needs an interface, backend, environments and a delivery process. When infrastructure and DevOps processes are not yet established, these components must be built and coordinated from scratch.

chapters.label: SOLUTION
chapters.title:
Service workflows
in one place
chapters.text: The interface brings platform workflows together, while automation handles repeated cloud and environment operations. Working with the application and its infrastructure becomes a connected process.

chapters.label: HOW IT WORKS
chapters.title:
From user action
to running service
chapters.text: The interface connects users to platform services. Scripts handle cloud operations, environments are defined in code, and changes follow a shared delivery process. Operations can be repeated without manually recreating settings.
chapters.note: Next.js · Terraform · Ansible · Kubernetes · Argo CD

chapters.label: OUTCOME
chapters.title:
Service management
without routine manual work
chapters.text: A single interface for working with services, automated cloud operations and repeatable deployment. Less manual maintenance means more time for product development.

name: LLMOps
title:
An AI service
you can operate
summary: An internal AI assistant in your own infrastructure: shared model access, controlled load and quality checks before release. Reference architecture.

chapters.label: PROBLEM
chapters.title:
The prototype works.
What comes next?
chapters.text: An AI assistant answers test prompts, but daily use requires more: application access, load limits, error diagnosis and a way to check whether a new model or prompt makes answers worse.

chapters.label: SOLUTION
chapters.title:
A shared foundation
for LLM operations
chapters.text: Teams connect applications through a shared gateway with application identities and access policies. Models run in the company’s Kubernetes cluster; configuration and prompts are versioned. Changes are evaluated before rollout, so adding AI does not create a separate, unmanaged service for every team.
chapters.note: Kubernetes · Kong Gateway Enterprise · AI Proxy Advanced · vLLM

chapters.label: HOW IT WORKS
chapters.title:
From request
to evaluated release
chapters.text: The gateway validates access and routes requests to the model. Metrics show latency, errors and load, while traces help investigate answers. Before release, the new version is compared with the previous one on agreed test inputs; quality and latency thresholds are defined for the use case.
chapters.note: OIDC · AI Rate Limiting Advanced · Langfuse · Prometheus · Grafana

chapters.label: OUTCOME
chapters.title:
AI operations
under team control
chapters.text: The target design provides controlled access, visible load and a clear update process. Teams can evaluate changes before release and investigate issues using operational data. This is a reference architecture: quality, performance and cost must be validated in a pilot.

details.title: Pilot scenario
details.text: Reference design: a text assistant with vLLM in Kubernetes and a self-managed Kong Gateway Enterprise with licensed AI plugins. Corporate identity and application policies control access; the inference endpoint is not exposed directly. Langfuse collects application traces and evaluation results inside the same environment. A pilot validates quality, p95 latency, time to first token, GPU use and recovery after a failure. Token limits are not a GPU cost estimate. Model licensing, gateway subscription availability, hardware, data masking and retention must be agreed before implementation.

name: Kubernetes & CI/CD
title:
Less manual work.
More stable services.
summary: Changes without repeated manual setup, clear deployment workflows and visibility into service health.

chapters.label: PROBLEM
chapters.title:
Manual operations
slow down change
chapters.text: When configuration is applied manually, every change takes engineering time and attention. Fragmented settings and recurring failures increase the maintenance burden and pull teams away from developing services.

chapters.label: SOLUTION
chapters.title:
Infrastructure
as a managed system
chapters.text: Infrastructure and service configuration is defined in code, with changes delivered through CI/CD. Deployment, monitoring and access management form a shared operational process.

chapters.label: HOW IT WORKS
chapters.title:
Changes
under control
chapters.text: Configuration is defined in code and applied through a pipeline. Applications follow shared deployment standards, with monitoring tracking their health afterwards. When something fails, alerts draw attention and logs help identify the cause.
chapters.note: Terraform · Ansible · GitLab CI · Kubernetes · Helm · Grafana · ELK

details.title: Example: Sentry reliability
details.text: Diagnosis linked Snuba consumer failures to disk blocking during backups. Restarts, monitoring and Grafana alerts helped restore stable operation, and the previous outages stopped interrupting developers.

chapters.label: OUTCOME
chapters.title:
Less routine work.
More control.
chapters.text: Configuration as code, repeatable deployment and visibility into service health. Fewer manual steps and a clear maintenance process help infrastructure evolve beyond recurring incident response.

name: Developer platform
title:
From code
to service
summary: Shared builds, quality checks and deployment for Python, .NET and Node.js teams.

chapters.label: PROBLEM
chapters.title:
Every service needs
a different guide
chapters.text: Different pipelines and deployment methods complicate project onboarding. Without shared standards, teams must repeatedly work out software delivery and operational configuration.

chapters.label: SOLUTION
chapters.title:
Shared standards,
different applications
chapters.text: New services adopt an established build, check and deployment workflow. Stack-specific requirements are handled in configuration, while delivery and maintenance remain consistent across the team.
chapters.note: GitLab CI · Jenkins · Helm · Python · .NET · Node.js

chapters.label: HOW IT WORKS
chapters.title:
A clear path
for every change
chapters.text: Each change follows a shared workflow for building, quality checks and deployment. New projects adopt existing delivery standards, with automatic synchronization to code analysis. After deployment, logs and monitoring help teams understand service behavior and locate the source of problems.

chapters.label: OUTCOME
chapters.title:
A new service.
A familiar process.
chapters.text: An established path from code to a running service: builds, quality checks and deployment follow shared standards. Less repeated setup when launching projects means more focus on development. Teams use different stacks while keeping a consistent approach to delivery and maintenance.

name: Anti-DDoS & resilience
title:
Clear actions
during an attack
summary: Automated anti-DDoS service operations and documented incident response procedures.

chapters.label: PROBLEM
chapters.title:
Attacks create
more manual work
chapters.text: During a network attack, engineers must monitor the application while operating protection tools. Manual tasks add pressure precisely when a clear sequence of actions matters.

chapters.label: SOLUTION
chapters.title:
Automation
with clear procedures
chapters.text: Repeated protection-service operations move into scripts. Monitoring, alerts and documented scenarios connect problem detection with concrete response actions.

chapters.label: HOW IT WORKS
chapters.title:
From signal
to action
chapters.text: An alert flags the problem, a prepared scenario defines the response, and scripts handle repeated operations with protection services. Engineers can move to action without assembling a procedure from scratch during an attack.

chapters.label: OUTCOME
chapters.title:
Fewer steps
at a critical moment
chapters.text: Prepared scenarios and automated protection-service operations reduce the operational burden during an attack. More attention goes to system health and decisions, with less spent on repetitive tasks.
